summary:
Guernsey is a self-governing Crown Dependency with its own parliament, the States of Guernsey, and its own statute book. The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and the single-sex-services code issued under it in 2025 do not apply here automatically. Local law governs, and United Kingdom measures reach Guernsey only by Order in Council.

Guernsey's criminal law has decriminalised same-sex sexual activity since before 1983, when the age of consent was set at 21 in line with the United Kingdom. The male same-sex age of consent fell to 18 in 2000 and was equalised at 16 by legislation approved in 2011 that took effect on 5 November 2012. The island nonetheless retains specific male homosexual offences, including a ban on homosexual sexual acts not conducted in private, which can expose men to prosecution for conduct that is lawful elsewhere.

Transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 2007, including obtaining a new birth certificate. Guernsey law permits only the issue of a new birth certificate and does not amend or remove entries from the existing record, so prior gender markers remain visible on the original document.

On 10 December 2015 the States of Guernsey approved same-sex marriage by 37 votes to 7. Two alternatives were rejected as insufficient: a civil-partnership-only scheme, and a single secular status called Union Civile that would have applied to all couples alike. The enabling legislation was left to a separate bill, which commenced in 2018. Guernsey is the only part of the British Isles never to have enacted civil-partnership legislation of its own, though United Kingdom civil partnerships have been recognised for succession purposes since 2 April 2012.

Family recognition moved earlier the same year. A review of the Adoption Law, recorded at page 1170 of the States of Guernsey Billet d'État of 24 June 2015, ended a fifty-year bar on unmarried couples adopting; the States agreed that same-sex couples may adopt, that civil partnerships are recognised in adoption proceedings, and that both partners hold equal parental responsibility.

Guernsey adopted the United Kingdom's relaxed blood-donor rules on 23 September 2011, making gay andbisexual men eligible after a twelve-month deferral from around 7 November 2011, ending a local ban dating from the 1980s HIV era. Other donation restrictions were unchanged.

Discrimination protections were built up in stages. A 2004 law enabled the States of Guernsey to pass Ordinances banning discrimination, and the Sex Discrimination (Employment) (Guernsey) Ordinance, 2005 prohibited discrimination based on gender identity in employment. As of 2020 no equivalent Ordinance had outlawed discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. Protections covering sexual orientation and gender identity existed in child welfare proceedings in Guernsey and Alderney since 2008 and in Sark since 2016. In September 2022 the States passed a comprehensive anti-discrimination bill unanimously, by 33 votes to 0, explicitly including sexual orientation and rejecting proposed exemptions for businesses of five employees or fewer and for religious affiliations. It took effect on 1 October 2023.
tangentialFactors:
Guernsey's adoption reform followed the same change in neighbouring Jersey by two days, indicating a coordinated Channel Islands movement rather than an isolated local decision.

The 2015 marriage debate was described as extremely positive, and the advocacy charity Liberate called it a historic day; there is no record of organised opposition of the kind seen in larger jurisdictions.

The blood-donor rule change was adopted deliberately to match the United Kingdom's own timetable, a pattern that also explains how other British standards reach the island without formal extension.

Guernsey's retention of a specific offence governing where homosexual acts take place, alongside an equalised age of consent, means the island's statute book carries residual provisions that other British jurisdictions have repealed in full.
localsOnly:
Employment discrimination on the basis of gender identity has been prohibited since the Sex Discrimination (Employment) (Guernsey) Ordinance, 2005, made under the enabling law of 2004. The comprehensive anti-discrimination legislation passed unanimously in September 2022 extended protection across the board and took effect on 1 October 2023.

Child welfare proceedings have applied anti-discrimination protections covering sexual orientation and gender identity in Guernsey and Alderney since 2008, and in Sark since 2016.

Residents changing gender receive a new birth certificate; the original record is not amended, so prior entries persist on the earlier document.

Les Nicolles, the island's only prison, opened in 1989 and is operated by the States of Guernsey. It holds male, female and vulnerable prisoners of juvenile and adult ages across 11 wings, with a capacity of 139; it held about 99 prisoners in November 2024.
outOfScopeNotes:
No recorded rule governs whether Les Nicolles houses prisoners by birth sex or gender identity, and no source documents a separate unit, solitary confinement, or segregation practice for transgender prisoners there. This is an absence in the available material, not a finding of safety or of risk.

No source in this inventory addresses access to gender-affirming healthcare on the island, waiting times, or referral pathways to the United Kingdom.

No source documents hate-crime reporting rates, police recording practice, or prosecutions with a transgender victim in Guernsey.

Whether the residual offence on non-private homosexual conduct has been used in prosecution, or remains a dead-letter provision, is not sourced here.

The practical application of the 2023 anti-discrimination regime to gender identity in services beyond employment is not evidenced in this inventory.
